Episode 10, Wandering Rocks, is built from 19 short vignettes of Dubliners moving through the city at the same moment. The narrative jumps rapidly from one micro‑scene to another. This passage is part of the Cunningham–Power–Wyse Nolan sequence, as they walk toward James Kavanagh’s winerooms to gather contributions for the Dignam family.

“Outside la Maison Claire Blazes Boylan waylaid Jack Mooney’s brother‑in‑law, humpy, tight, making for the liberties.”

• Boylan appears for a moment — swaggering, sociable, always stopping people on the street. • He “waylays” (stops) Jack Mooney’s brother‑in‑law, who is described as:• humpy — hunched or stooped • tight — drunk
• making for the liberties — heading toward the Liberties district of Dublin This is typical Wandering Rocks: characters intersect briefly, then peel away.
“John Wyse Nolan fell back with Mr Power…”
Wyse Nolan slows his pace to walk beside Power. They’re reading and discussing the subscription list for the Dignam family.
“…while Martin Cunningham took the elbow of a dapper little man in a shower of hail suit…”
Cunningham, always the diplomat and helper, gently guides a small, well‑dressed man wearing a “shower of hail” suit — a speckled or patterned fabric.
“…who walked uncertainly, with hasty steps past Micky Anderson’s watches.”
The man is walking awkwardly and quickly, passing Micky Anderson’s watch shop on Parliament Street. We soon learn why:

“The assistant town clerk’s corns are giving him some trouble,” Wyse Nolan explains.
The man’s painful feet make him walk in those “hasty,” uneven steps.

1. Street choreography
Joyce shows Dublin as a living organism — people crossing paths, stopping each other, drifting in and out of view.
2. Character micro‑portraits
Each figure is sketched in a few strokes:

• Boylan: confident, intrusive, always talking • Mooney’s brother‑in‑law: drunk, shabby • The assistant town clerk: neat but physically uncomfortable • Cunningham: helpful, steady
• Power and Wyse Nolan: following, observing
3. Social texture
The passage shows:

• casual street encounters
• small civic roles (assistant town clerk) • the geography of Dublin (Maison Claire, Parliament Street, Anderson’s watches) • the charitable mission of Cunningham’s group
4. The cinematic style of Wandering Rocks
This episode is Joyce’s most “camera‑like” writing: quick cuts, brief shots, characters entering and exiting frame.
🧠 Why this matters in the larger narrative
Boylan’s appearance here is important because:
• he is on his way to Molly Bloom at 4 p.m. • Joyce sprinkles him through the city like a shadow over Bloom’s day • his casual dominance contrasts with Bloom’s anxious avoidance

Meanwhile, Cunningham’s group continues their kindness mission, reinforcing the theme of Dublin’s moral cross‑currents: generosity, drunkenness, vanity, pain, gossip, and civic duty all happening simultaneously.

blocks.label: The overture, line by line
paras:
Takeaway:
This is one of the most famous sound‑drunk, music‑saturated passages in Sirens. Joyce is showing Lenehan (bronze) and Miss Kennedy (gold) sitting in the Ormond Hotel bar, hearing Boylan’s horse outside, reacting to flirtation, and being swept up in the musical atmosphere. The language is deliberately fragmented, rhythmic, and sensual — it imitates musical motifs, erotic tension, and the “seduction” theme of the episode.
Below is a clear, line‑by‑line explanation.
🎵 Context: The Sirens episode
Everything in Sirens is written as music — motifs, riffs, echoes, repeated syllables, onomatopoeia. Characters are described not realistically but as instruments:

• Bronze = Miss Douce
• Gold = Miss Kennedy
Their hair colors become musical timbres. Their reactions are rendered as sound.
Boylan is approaching the Ormond Hotel on his way to Molly. His presence creates erotic vibration in the room.
🧩 Line‑by‑line explanation
“Bronze by gold heard the hoofirons, steelyringing / Imperthnthn thnthnthn.”
Miss Douce (bronze) and Miss Kennedy (gold) hear Boylan’s horse outside. The hoofbeats are rendered musically:
• “hoofirons, steelyringing” — metallic rhythm • “Imperthnthn thnthnthn” — Joyce’s onomatopoeic imitation of the horse’s trot
This is the Boylan motif: confident, sexual, rhythmic.
“Chips, picking chips off rocky thumbnail, chips.”
This is Lenehan, fidgeting, picking at his nails. Joyce turns the tiny gesture into a percussive sound: chips chips chips.
It’s part of the episode’s technique: every movement becomes music.
“Horrid! And gold flushed more.”
Miss Kennedy (gold) reacts with a blush — perhaps to Boylan’s arrival, perhaps to Lenehan’s crude behavior. “Horrid!” is her prim, ladylike protest.
Her blush is described as gold flushing — again, color as musical tone.
“A husky fifenote blew.”
A musician in the bar plays a fife — a small flute. The sound is “husky,” sensual, breathy.
This is another musical motif entering the texture of the scene.
“Blew. Blue bloom is on the.”
Joyce riffs on the word blew → blue → Bloom.
This is a pun on the Irish song “Bluebells are Blooming” and on Bloom himself.
It’s a musical fragment that will complete itself later (“Blue bloom is on the gold pinnacled hair”).
The syntax breaks because Joyce is imitating melodic anticipation — a phrase waiting for resolution.
“Goldpinnacled hair.”
Miss Kennedy’s hair again — “gold pinnacled,” like a shining tower.
The phrase completes the earlier fragment:
Blue bloom is on the gold pinnacled hair
This is a musical line, a lyric, a motif. It fuses:

• Bloom’s name
• the color blue
• the golden hair of Miss Kennedy
• the erotic atmosphere of Boylan’s arrival
It’s a synesthetic chord: color + sound + desire.
🎯 What Joyce is doing here
1. Turning Dublin into music
Every sound — hoofbeats, fingernails, breath — becomes part of a score.
2. Sexual tension as musical vibration
Boylan’s approach is rendered as rhythm and metallic ringing. The women blush; the room vibrates.
3. Bloom’s name as a musical motif
“Blue bloom” is a pun, a lyric fragment, a sound‑shape.
4. Fragmentation = musical phrasing
The broken syntax imitates:

• riffs
• motifs
• anticipations
• resolutions
It’s not meant to be read as normal prose.
🧠 Emotional undercurrent

This passage captures the erotic electricity of Boylan’s presence — the women’s excitement, Lenehan’s nervous fidgeting, the musicians’ playing, and Bloom’s ghostly presence in the music even though he is not physically there.
It’s the soundscape of seduction.

blocks.label: Dublin men remember Molly
paras:
Short answer:
This is one of those Cyclops‑chapter pub‑banter passages where Simon Dedalus and the men riff on Molly Bloom’s past, half‑remembering, half‑inventing, and half‑leering. It’s a swirl of gossip, misremembered biography, music‑hall references, and sexual innuendo, all delivered in the deliberately chaotic, parodic style of the episode.
🧩 What’s happening in the scene

You’re in Episode 12, “Cyclops,” inside Barney Kiernan’s pub. The narration is split between the anonymous “citizen” narrator and the parodic interpolations. The men are talking about Molly Bloom, but in the way Dublin men talk:

• fragmentary
• boastful
• inaccurate
• tinged with erotic curiosity
• and always with a performative “I knew her when…”
Simon Dedalus is the loudest voice here, puffing his pipe and dredging up scraps of Molly’s early life.
🧠 Breaking down the references
“Mrs Marion Bloom has left off clothes of all descriptions.”
A crude joke implying Molly is sexually available or immodest. This is pub‑room misogyny, not fact.
“Jingle jaunted down the quays. Blazes sprawled on bounding tyres.”
A rapid‑fire montage of Boylan (“Jingle”) and Blazes Boylan (“Blazes”), Molly’s lover. It’s Joyce’s cinematic cutaway: the men gossip, and the narration flashes to Boylan moving through Dublin.
“Smell of burn. Of Paul de Kock.”
Paul de Kock was a French novelist known for light erotic fiction. The implication: Molly’s world has a whiff of sensuality.
“A buxom lassy. Marion … —Tweedy.”
They’re trying to remember her maiden name: Marion Tweedy. This is correct.
“Is she alive? —And kicking.”

A stock comic exchange.
Also a hint that Molly is still vigorous, sensual, not fading.
“Daughter of the regiment.”
A reference to Donizetti’s opera La fille du régiment. It’s a way of mythologizing Molly’s past—turning her into a kind of theatrical figure.
“I remember the old drummajor.”
Simon claims to remember her father’s military connections. This is part memory, part invention.
“Buccinator muscle is … My Irish Molly, O.”

Simon tries to recall anatomical trivia (the buccinator is a cheek muscle), then slips into singing “My Irish Molly, O,” a popular music‑hall song. He’s conflating Molly Bloom with the song’s archetype: the lively Irish girl.
“From the rock of Gibraltar… all the way.”

A nod to Molly’s birthplace: Gibraltar.
This is one of the few accurate biographical details in the whole exchange.
🎯 What Joyce is doing here
This passage is a collage of male memory, fantasy, and bravado. Joyce uses:

• misremembered facts
• music‑hall songs
• military clichés
• sexual innuendo
• comic exaggeration
to show how Molly exists in Dublin’s collective imagination—not as a real woman, but as a mythic, eroticized figure assembled from scraps of rumor.
It’s also a contrast with Bloom’s own interior tenderness toward her. The men flatten her into a stereotype; Bloom sees her as a complex human being.
🧵 The emotional undercurrent

Under the jokes, there’s a subtle cruelty: Molly is being discussed as a public property, a figure of gossip. Bloom is present in the pub, hearing his wife turned into a caricature. This is part of the humiliation‑thread running through Ulysses—the city’s collective imagination intruding on Bloom’s private life.

blocks.label: The street cries, sentence by sentence
paras: Here is a sentence‑by‑sentence explanation of your passage, focused specifically on how each fragment works inside the Sirens episode, where Joyce turns language itself into music — onomatopoeia, rhythm, motif, echo, and associative drift. Citations refer to the sources used for the musical‑stylistic context of Sirens.  American ... +1
🎼 The passage in context

This section comes from the musical overture and early middle of Sirens, where Bloom’s thoughts, street noises, remembered songs, and erotic associations all blend into a fugue‑like texture. Joyce compresses motifs: Molly, Boylan’s jingling, street cries, opera, sexual memory, loneliness, Dignam’s funeral, the whore, and Bloom’s embarrassment.
I’ll take each two‑sentence unit and explain what’s happening musically and narratively.
🎵 “Molly in her shift in Lombard street west, hair down.
I suppose each kind of trade made its own, don’t you see?”

• Bloom flashes to an erotic memory of Molly in her shift, hair loose — a sensual image. • “Lombard Street West” is where they lived early in their marriage; this is nostalgic and sexual. • The second sentence shifts abruptly: Bloom generalizes about street cries and signals — each trade having its own sound. This anticipates the coming catalogue of noises.
Sirens effect: sudden modulation from erotic memory to sound‑catalogue; associative drift.
🎵 “Hunter with a horn. Haw. Have you the? Cloche. Sonne la.”

• Bloom lists trade‑calls: hunters blow horns; “Haw” is the horn’s sound. • “Have you the?” is a fragment of a street vendor’s cry. • “Cloche / Sonne la” refers to Miss Douce snapping her garter like a bell (“Sonnez la cloche!”), a motif in Sirens representing flirtation and sexual display.  American Lit...
Sirens effect: musical onomatopoeia; eroticized bell imagery.
🎵 “Shepherd his pipe. Pwee little wee.”
• Shepherds traditionally pipe to call sheep; Bloom imagines the sound. • “Pwee little wee” imitates the tiny flute‑like note — a motif in the overture (“a husky fifenote blew”).  American Lit...
Sirens effect: Joyce turns pastoral piping into literal musical notation.
🎵 “Policeman a whistle. Locks and keys! Sweep!”
• More street cries: policeman’s whistle; locksmith’s call; chimney sweep’s cry. • Joyce compresses Dublin’s soundscape into rhythmic fragments.
Sirens effect: urban soundscape becomes orchestral instrumentation.
🎵 “Four o’clock’s all’s well! Sleep! All is lost now.”
• “All’s well!” is the night‑watchman’s cry. • “Sleep!” echoes lullaby or night‑call. • “All is lost now” is a motif from the opera La Sonnambula, which appears repeatedly in Sirens.  American Lit...
Sirens effect: Joyce blends street‑cry with operatic lament.
🎵 “Drum? Pompedy. Wait. I know.”
• Bloom hears or imagines a drumbeat (“Pompedy”). • “Wait. I know.” signals Bloom recognizing a pattern — the musical logic of the noises.
Sirens effect: rhythmic percussion; Bloom’s mind trying to impose order on the fugue.
🎵 “Towncrier, bumbailiff. Long John. Waken the dead. Pom.”

• More cries: town crier; bailiff.
• “Long John” may be a nickname or comic cry. • “Waken the dead” exaggerates the loudness. • “Pom” is a drumbeat.
Sirens effect: crescendo of public cries; percussive repetition.
🎵 “Dignam. Poor little nominedomine. Pom.”
• Bloom’s mind jumps to Paddy Dignam’s funeral (“nominedomine” = Latin prayer fragment). • “Pom” again is the drumbeat — funeral drum, military drum, or simply rhythmic thought.
Sirens effect: grief motif enters the musical texture.
🎵 “It is music. I mean of course it’s all pom pom pom very much what they call da capo.”

• Bloom explicitly recognizes the musical structure of his thoughts. • “Da capo” means repeating from the beginning — fitting the fugue structure of Sirens. • The “pom pom pom” is the rhythmic motif of the episode.
Sirens effect: self‑awareness of musical form.
🎵 “Still you can hear. As we march, we march along, march along. Pom.”

• Bloom imagines a marching rhythm.
• The repetition mimics a marching song. • “Pom” is the beat.
Sirens effect: Joyce turns Bloom’s inner monologue into a literal march.
🎵 “I must really. Fff. Now if I did that at a banquet.”
• Bloom imagines himself making a noise (“Fff”) — perhaps blowing or hissing. • He thinks how inappropriate it would be at a banquet — comic self‑consciousness.
Sirens effect: comic interruption of the musical flow.
🎵 “Just a question of custom shah of Persia. Breathe a prayer, drop a tear.”
• Bloom recalls exotic customs (Shah of Persia) — a typical Bloomish associative leap. • “Breathe a prayer, drop a tear” sounds like sentimental song lyrics.
Sirens effect: ornamental, operatic sentimentality.
🎵 “All the same he must have been a bit of a natural not to see it was a yeoman cap. Muffled up.”

• Bloom recalls someone at Dignam’s funeral who misidentified a cap. • “Natural” = simpleton.
• “Muffled up” refers to funeral attire.
Sirens effect: return of funeral motif.
🎵 “Wonder who was that chap at the grave in the brown macin. O, the whore of the lane!”
• Bloom wonders about a man in a brown mackintosh — a recurring mystery figure in Ulysses. • Sudden shift: Bloom remembers the whore in the lane, a sexual memory.
Sirens effect: abrupt modulation from funeral to erotic.
🎵 “A frowsy whore with black straw sailor hat askew came glazily in the day along the quay towards Mr Bloom.”
• Description of the prostitute Bloom once encountered. • “Frowsy” = shabby; “glazily” = bleary‑eyed.
Sirens effect: visual motif of a “fallen woman,” paralleling the Sirens theme.  Yale University
🎵 “When first he saw that form endearing? Yes, it is. I feel so lonely.”
• Bloom remembers first seeing her; he questions whether he found her endearing. • “I feel so lonely” is Bloom’s emotional core — loneliness is a major Sirens motif.
Sirens effect: lyrical melancholy.
🎵 “Wet night in the lane. Horn. Who had the?”

• Memory of the encounter: a wet night.
• “Horn” may refer to a street‑sound or sexual pun. • “Who had the?” is an unfinished thought — typical of Bloom’s associative drift.
Sirens effect: fragmentary recall, like broken musical phrases.
🎵 “Heehaw shesaw. Off her beat here.”
• Onomatopoeia (“Heehaw shesaw”) — donkey‑like sound, mocking or rhythmic. • “Off her beat here” means she’s working outside her usual area.
Sirens effect: comic musicality; rhythmic nonsense syllables.
🎵 “What is she? Hope she. Psst! Any chance of your wash. Knew Molly.”

• Bloom wonders about her situation.
• “Any chance of your wash” = she’s soliciting laundry work (common euphemism for prostitution). • “Knew Molly” — Bloom realizes she knew his wife.
Sirens effect: final chord: erotic memory, shame, Molly’s presence.
🎼 Summary of what Joyce is doing
Across these fragments Joyce:

• builds a fugue of Dublin noises, erotic memories, funeral echoes, and operatic motifs. • uses onomatopoeia (“pom,” “pwee,” “heehaw”) as musical notes. • blends public cries with private emotion, showing Bloom’s mind as an orchestra. • interweaves Molly, Boylan, Dignam, and the whore into one musical texture. • creates a rhythmic, non‑linear narrative, characteristic of Sirens.

paras: Bloom continues, identifying himself with the Jewish race in addition to his Irish nationality, and states that his race suffers from hate, persecution, and injustice.  John Wyse Nolan suggests the Jews stand up for themselves with force, but Bloom rejects this solution on very simple yet profound grounds: “Force, hatred, history, all that. blocks.label: Gerty and Portrait’s birdgirl
paras: It is worth noting the echoes between the Bloom/Gerty encounter and the birdgirl scene at the end of Chapter IV in A Portrait: Stephen is walking along the beach alone, resolving to pursue a life of artistic creation when he comes across a young woman standing in the water. She was alone and still, gazing out to sea; and when she felt his presence and the worship of his gaze her eyes turned to him in quiet suffrance of his gaze, without shame or wantonness [...] and a faint flame trembled on her cheek. (Portrait 186) At the risk of belaboring the point, both Stephen and Bloom stare worshipfully at girls on the beach, both Gerty and the birdgirl blush and allow them to stare; both women are described in terms of delicacy and “ivorylike purity;” they both wear blue; in both scenes the “lightclad figures of children and girls and voices childish and girlish in the air” (P 185); and, in echoes yet to come in “Nausicaa”, the words “hither, thither” appear and skirts are “bared almost to the hips.”  Joyce here seems to be ironically mocking Stephen as well as his younger self as an author as well as drawing parallels in order to highlight the differences between the two protagonists’ reactions to these similar encounters.

paras:
But who was Gerty?
Gerty MacDowell who was seated near her
companions, lost in thought, gazing far away into the distance was, in very truth, as fair a specimen of winsome Irish girlhood as one could wish to see. She was pronounced beautiful by all who knew her though, as folks often said, she was more a Giltrap than a MacDowell. Her figure was slight and graceful, inclining even to fragility but those iron jelloids she had been taking of late had done her a world of good much better than the Widow Welch’s female pills and she was much better of those discharges she used to get and that tired feeling. The waxen pallor of her face was almost spiritual in its ivorylike purity though her rosebud mouth was a genuine Cupid’s bow, Greekly perfect. Her hands were of finely veined alabaster with tapering fingers and as white as lemonjuice and queen of ointments could make them though it was not true that she used to wear kid gloves in bed or take a milk footbath either. Bertha Supple told that once to Edy Boardman, a deliberate lie, when she was black out at daggers drawn with Gerty (the girl chums had of course their little tiffs from time to time like the rest of mortals) and she told her not to let on whatever she did that it was her that told her or she’d never speak to her again. No. Honour where honour is due. There was an innate refinement, a languid queenly hauteur about Gerty which was unmistakably evidenced in her delicate hands and higharched instep. Had kind fate but willed her to be born a gentlewoman of high degree in her own right and had she only received the benefit of a good education Gerty MacDowell might easily have held her own beside any lady in the land and have seen herself exquisitely gowned with jewels on her brow and patrician suitors at her feet vying with one another to pay their devoirs to her. Mayhap it was this, the love that might have been, that lent to her softlyfeatured face at whiles a look, tense with suppressed meaning, that imparted a strange yearning tendency to the beautiful eyes, a charm few could resist. blocks.label: The prophetic voice and the cuckold
paras: The prophetic‑biblical passage absolutely does relate to Bloom’s cuckold identity, but Joyce encodes it indirectly — through stylistic parody, national allegory, and Bloom’s own psychology. This is one of the places where Oxen of the Sun quietly folds Bloom’s sexual humiliation into a larger mythic frame.
⭐ Core takeaway

The biblical voice rebuking “Erin” mirrors Bloom’s internal sense of being betrayed, being supplanted by a “stranger,” and being made to witness his own displacement — exactly what happens with Molly and Boylan. Joyce uses national prophecy as a metaphor for Bloom’s private cuckold pain.
📜 1. The prophetic voice = Bloom’s wounded conscience
The passage:
“Erin… thou broughtedst in a stranger to my gates to commit fornication in my sight…”

is not just about Ireland.
It is also about Bloom, because:

• Bloom = the “husband” whose covenant has been broken • Molly = the nation who “waxed fat and kicked like Jeshurum” • Boylan = the “stranger brought to the gates” • Bloom’s humiliation = the “fornication in my sight”
Joyce fuses national betrayal with marital betrayal.
Bloom’s humiliation is recast in biblical terms: he is the God‑figure whose beloved has taken another man into the marital home.
🏠 2. “A stranger to my gates” = Boylan entering 7 Eccles Street
This line is the clearest cuckold parallel.
In biblical prophecy, “bringing a stranger into the gates” is a metaphor for infidelity.
In Ulysses, it is literal:

• Boylan goes to Bloom’s house
• Boylan enters Molly’s bedroom
• Bloom knows it
• Bloom imagines it
• Bloom is humiliated by it
The biblical style exaggerates Bloom’s pain into cosmic proportions.
🔥 3. “To commit fornication in my sight” = Bloom’s voyeuristic masochism
Bloom’s cuckold identity is not only painful — it is charged, complicated, and sometimes eroticized.
Joyce repeatedly shows Bloom:

• imagining Molly with Boylan
• picturing their bodies
• replaying the sounds
• lingering on details
• experiencing humiliation as a mix of pain and fascination
The biblical voice dramatizes this dynamic:
Bloom is forced to “see” the betrayal, just as the prophet sees Israel’s sins.

This is why Joyce chooses prophecy:
prophets are compelled witnesses.
Bloom is a compelled witness to Molly’s affair.
🧬 4. “Wax fat and kick like Jeshurum” = Molly’s sexual vitality
Jeshurun (Israel) becomes prosperous, proud, and rebellious.
Joyce uses this to gesture toward Molly’s:

• sexual confidence
• independence
• appetite
• refusal to be constrained by Bloom’s passivity

Bloom is gentle, quiet, inward.
Molly is expansive, sensual, outward.
The biblical metaphor frames Molly’s sexuality as something powerful, almost mythic — and Bloom’s cuckoldry as part of a larger drama of desire and rebellion.
🧩 5. Why Joyce hides Bloom’s cuckoldry inside national prophecy
Because Oxen of the Sun is about:

• fertility
• lineage
• creation
• the evolution of language
• the birth of nations
• the birth of children
• the birth of styles
Bloom’s cuckold identity becomes one more “birth” — a psychological creation shaped by:

• Ireland’s political subjugation
• Bloom’s social marginalization
• Bloom’s marital displacement
• Bloom’s erotic imagination
Joyce blends:

Ireland betrayed by outsiders
with
Bloom betrayed by Boylan
to show how personal and national humiliation intertwine.
🎯 In plain modern terms
The biblical passage is a stylized way of saying:

Bloom feels like Molly has brought Boylan into their home to have sex, and he feels humiliated, betrayed, and strangely compelled to witness it — just like a prophet watching his nation betray its God.

blocks.label: Greater love: a mock-gospel of cuckoldry
paras: This is one of the sharpest, most overtly cuckold‑themed moments in Oxen of the Sun, and Joyce frames it in a deliberately parodic gospel‑Nietzschean style to make Bloom’s humiliation both cosmic and comic. You’ve now reached the point where the episode stops hinting and starts declaring Bloom’s cuckold identity in mythic, philosophical, and satirical registers.
⭐ Core meaning

The passage is a mock‑scriptural, mock‑Nietzschean justification of cuckoldry, with Bloom as the “man” who lays down his wife for his friend — Boylan. It’s a joke, a prophecy, a moral inversion, and a psychological truth all at once.
📜 “Greater love than this… no man hath that a man lay down his wife for his friend.”
This is a parody of the Gospel of John:
“Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.”
Joyce twists it:
Bloom doesn’t lay down his life — he lays down his wife.
This is the most explicit, comedic formulation of Bloom’s cuckoldry in the entire novel.
It suggests:

• Bloom’s passivity
• Bloom’s generosity
• Bloom’s masochistic acceptance
• Bloom’s willingness to let Boylan have Molly • Bloom’s strange, inverted “self‑sacrifice”
It’s both a joke and a psychological truth: Bloom does allow the affair to happen.
🧠 “Thus, or words to that effect, saith Zarathustra…”
Joyce invokes Nietzsche’s Zarathustra — the prophet of self‑overcoming, inversion of values, and radical revaluation of morality.
But Joyce turns him into:
“regius professor of French letters to the university of Oxtail”

This is pure parody.
Zarathustra becomes a pompous academic at a ridiculous university.
Why Nietzsche here?
Because Nietzsche is the philosopher of:

• overturning traditional morality
• embracing humiliation
• transforming suffering into strength
• accepting the eternal recurrence of one’s fate
Bloom’s cuckoldry becomes a philosophical doctrine — a comic “ethic” of self‑sacrifice.
🏰 “Bring a stranger within thy tower…”
This line returns to the biblical‑prophetic mode you saw earlier.
The “tower” = the marital home, 7 Eccles Street. The “stranger” = Boylan.
This is the same metaphor as:

• “a stranger to my gates”
• “fornication in my sight”
Joyce is repeating the cuckold motif in different historical styles.
🛏️ “…it will go hard but thou wilt have the secondbest bed.”
This is the punchline.
The “secondbest bed” is a Shakespeare reference: in his will, Shakespeare left his wife Anne Hathaway the second‑best bed.
Joyce uses it as a cuckold joke:

If you bring a stranger into your home,
you won’t be sleeping in the best bed anymore.

Boylan gets the best bed — Molly’s bed.
Bloom gets the second‑best bed — figuratively and literally.
This is the entire cuckold dynamic compressed into one line.
🔥 How this ties directly to Bloom’s psychology
This passage crystallizes Bloom’s cuckold identity in four ways:
1. Moral inversion
Bloom’s humiliation is framed as “greater love.”
2. Philosophical justification
Nietzsche is invoked to make cuckoldry sound like a heroic act of self‑overcoming.
3. Biblical prophecy
Bloom’s displacement becomes a mythic betrayal.
4. Domestic reality
Boylan gets Molly’s bed; Bloom gets the “secondbest.”
Joyce blends:

• scripture
• philosophy
• comedy
• domestic realism
to show how Bloom’s cuckoldry is not just a plot point — it’s a mythic condition, a psychological structure, a lens through which Bloom experiences the world.
🎯 In plain modern terms
This passage is saying:

Bloom is the kind of man who would give up his wife to another man, and that makes him both ridiculous and strangely noble. Nietzsche would approve. Shakespeare would laugh. And Bloom ends up with the second‑best bed.

blocks.label: Eight drafts and half a year
paras: In early spring 1920, Joyce emerged from the 1,000 hours he had spent writing “Oxen” and turned his attention to “Circe.”  He expected that this episode, like the few he had recently composed, would take him two to three months to complete.  Little did he know that “Circe” would require eight drafts and take over half a year to write (Letters), much less that it would have the power to bewitch his creative process and entirely transform Ulysses.  This episode, with its exhaustive reprises of virtually every character, object, and idea introduced in the novel thus far, would compel Joyce to revise much of what he had previously written.  Joyce estimated that he wrote a third of Ulysses at the proof stage of the revision process (Beach 58)
As Karen Lawrence puts it, “‘Circe’ provides a stage for a libidinous release of tendencies in the language and in the characters” (Lawrence 150-51).

blocks.label: Stepaside, the ragman and the pocket check
paras:
In this sequence from the "Circe" episode, Bloom is navigating the dark, disorienting streets of "Nighttown." His internal monologue is a frantic mix of self-congratulation, civic duty, and sudden panic. 1. "In Darkest Stepaside"
Bloom recalls a moment of personal pride. He once got lost in Stepaside (a village south of Dublin). Instead of just complaining, he wrote a letter to the Irish Cyclist magazine titled "In Darkest Stepaside" (a play on Henry Morton Stanley’s In Darkest Africa). * The "Boon": He claims his letter convinced the Touring Club to put up a signpost. This shows Bloom’s "scientific" and "civic" mind; he wants to improve the world through organized, practical means. * "Keep to the right": He is literally giving himself directions to avoid getting lost again. 2. The Ragman and the "Fence"
Bloom looks at the ragman he just encountered and suspects him of being a "fence" (someone who buys and sells stolen goods). * The "First place murderer makes for": Bloom’s mind jumps to a dark, cinematic place. He imagines criminals hiding in the slums to "wash off" their sins—a metaphor for hiding evidence or blending into the grime of the city. 3. The Collision and the "Weak Hams"
When the Caffrey children (who appeared earlier in the "Nausicaa" episode) run into him, Bloom is physically shaken. * "Weak hams": This is Joyce’s humorous way of saying Bloom’s thighs/knees went weak from the shock. * The Pocket Check: He immediately frantically pats his various pockets to ensure his belongings are still there. 4. The Inventory of Bloom's Soul
The items he checks are symbolic "relics" he has carried throughout the day: * Sweets of Sin: A "racy" novel he bought for his wife, Molly. * Potato: The "panacea" or lucky charm from his mother. * Soap: A bar of lemon soap he bought in the morning, which has been in his pocket all day, becoming a sort of talismanic object. 5. The "Old Thieves' Dodge"
Bloom’s immediate reaction to being bumped into is suspicion. He believes the collision wasn't an accident but a "dodge" (a trick). In Victorian and Edwardian urban lore, pickpockets would use children or "staged" collisions to distract a victim while they snatched a purse. This highlights Bloom’s outsider status—he feels like a target in this rough part of town. Summary of the Items in Bloom's Pockets
| Item | Significance |
|---|---|
| Watch fob | His connection to time and the orderly world. | | Pursepocket | His constant anxiety about money and being cheated. | | Sweets of Sin | His complex relationship with Molly and his own guilt. | | Potato/Soap | His connection to his heritage (mother) and his physical cleanliness/body. |

blocks.label: Othello, the minstrels and ‘someone in the house’
paras:
This passage is one of the most jarring and controversial moments in the "Circe" episode. It reflects the intersection of Molly’s sexual fantasies, colonial-era racial stereotypes, and Leopold Bloom’s own racial anxieties. 1. Molly's "Slumming" and the Exotic
Bloom begins by thinking of his wife, Molly. He imagines her desire to visit "Nighttown" (the slums) out of a sense of boredom or a craving for the "exotic." * "Negro servants in livery": Bloom recalls Molly’s fantasies of wealth and status, which, in 1904, often involved the racist trope of black servants as symbols of luxury. * Othello: He links this to Shakespeare’s Moor, whom he calls a "black brute," reflecting a common (and racist) interpretation of the play at the time, but also his personal insecurity about being a "cuckold" (like Othello). 2. The Minstrel Influence (The "Christies") Bloom’s mind jumps to the popular entertainment of the time: Blackface Minstrelsy. * Eugene Stratton: A famous white minstrel performer known for his "coon songs." * The Livermore Christies: A reference to the "Moore and Burgess Christie Minstrels," a popular troupe. * The Bohee Brothers: These were real-life African-American brothers (James and George Bohee) who were famous banjo players and performers in London and Dublin. 3. The Hallucination: Tom and Sam Bohee
In the dream-logic of Nighttown, the mentioned Bohee brothers instantly manifest. Joyce uses incredibly aggressive and stereotypical language here ("Sambo chokers," "nigger lips," "Kaffir eyes") to mirror the grotesque, dehumanizing way black people were portrayed in 1900s minstrel shows. * The Clothing: They appear in "white duck suits" and "scarlet socks"—stage costumes designed for high-contrast visual comedy. * The Dance: They perform a "breakdown" (a fast, rhythmic dance) in "clumsy clogs." This links back to the earlier mention of the "shoe trick"—the idea of feet and footwear as sources of anxiety or spectacle. 4. The Song: "Someone in the House with Dina" The lyrics they sing are a variation of the well-known American folk song "I've Been Working on the Railroad." * The Double Meaning: In the context of Ulysses, the lyrics "There's someone in the house with Dina" take on a paranoid meaning for Bloom. * The "Other Man": Throughout the day, Bloom has been tormented by the knowledge that Blazes Boylan is at his home with Molly. The "someone in the house" is Boylan. Even the hallucinatory minstrels are mocking Bloom’s status as a betrayed husband. Summary
This scene shows how Bloom’s brain "remixes" high culture (Othello), popular culture (the Bohee brothers), and his deepest fear (Molly's infidelity). The racist caricatures are used by Joyce to illustrate the ugly, distorted nature of the subconscious when it is under the pressure of guilt and jealousy.

paras: 🌒 What You’re Reading

This scene is from the “Circe” episode of Ulysses, where the narrative slips into a hallucinatory, nightmarish, theatrical mode. Reality bends. Characters morph. Internal guilt and fear take on physical form.
🧩 What’s Going On in the Scene
1. Bloom is being accused
The First Watchman thinks Bloom is carrying something dangerous (“infernal machine with a time fuse”). Bloom insists he was simply at a funeral.
2. The hallucination begins

A beagle suddenly transforms into the corpse-like apparition of Paddy Dignam, the man whose funeral Bloom attended earlier in the day. This grotesque metamorphosis is typical of the “Circe” episode—characters become symbols, fears become bodies.
3. Paddy Dignam’s ghost appears
The ghost confirms Bloom’s story: yes, it was his funeral. His appearance is intentionally horrific—gnawed, decayed, mutilated—reflecting:

• Bloom’s anxiety about death
• His guilt about his own voyeuristic curiosity • The chaotic, dreamlike logic of the brothel district
4. Bloom seizes the moment
Bloom triumphantly points out that even the dead are backing him up.
5. Paddy Dignam calls on Bloom

When he says “List, list, O list!” he’s echoing the ghost in Hamlet—a classic literary ghostly summons. He’s calling Bloom to listen, to pay attention, to receive some kind of revelation or confession.
🎭 Why It Matters
This moment blends:

• Comedy (a beagle turning into a corpse) • Horror (the mutilated ghost)
• Parody (Shakespearean ghost tropes)
• Psychological truth (Bloom’s guilt, fear, and desire for vindication)
It’s Joyce showing how Bloom’s inner life erupts into theatrical hallucination.

blocks.label: Infantilized under Zoe
paras: Concise takeaway

This moment in Circe stages Bloom’s humiliation by infantilizing him and placing him under the erotic, predatory control of Zoe and the brothel environment. Joyce fuses babyhood, sexuality, and shame to expose Bloom’s deepest anxieties about masculinity, agency, and desire.
What’s happening psychologically
1. Bloom is transformed into a baby
Joyce puts Bloom in babylinen, with a big head, lisping numbers. This is not just comic — it’s a ritual stripping of adult male identity.
Infantilization =

• no autonomy
• no sexual authority
• total vulnerability
• total dependency on women
This is one of Bloom’s recurring masochistic fantasies: to be relieved of responsibility by being reduced to a child.
2. Zoe becomes the controlling adult
Zoe’s “little parted talons” and the “secret monitor” touch are coded as:

• seductive
• manipulative
• authoritative
She is the one who leads, tests, and judges. Bloom is the one who follows, hesitates, trips, and is “saved.”
This reverses the gendered power dynamic Bloom feels he lacks in his marriage.
3. The buckles speak
The buckles chanting “Love me. Love me not. Love me.” externalize Bloom’s internal need for:

• approval
• affection
• erotic validation
It’s a childlike version of the adult erotic anxiety he carries everywhere.
4. The “male brutes” are the ghosts of her past lovers
The “lion reek” and the brutes roaring in the background represent:

• Bloom’s fear of sexual competition
• his sense of inadequacy
• his fascination with the men who have “possessed” Zoe
This is Joyce dramatizing Bloom’s cuckold imagination — not just with Molly, but with any sexually confident woman.
5. Bloom’s humiliation is pleasurable and terrifying
He is:

• lured
• tempted
• overwhelmed
• infantilized
• aroused
• ashamed
This is the exact blend Joyce uses throughout Circe to show Bloom’s erotic psychology: humiliation as a form of release.
Why this passage matters in the larger arc
This scene is one of the clearest examples of Joyce showing that Bloom’s erotic life is built around:

• submission
• loss of control
• being judged by women
• being compared to other men
• being reduced (child, animal, servant)
It’s not just kink — it’s a psychological mechanism for dealing with:

• guilt
• loneliness
• marital betrayal
• the burden of adulthood
Joyce turns all of that into theatrical hallucination.
One non‑obvious insight
Bloom’s baby‑form is not only humiliation — it’s also absolution.

As a baby, he cannot be blamed for desire. He cannot be blamed for Molly’s affair.
He cannot be blamed for his failures.
Infantilization is a way to escape guilt.

blocks.label: The catalogue of Bloom’s erotic objects
paras: 📚 What this passage means in context

This moment appears in the long catechistic inventory of Bloom’s possessions. Joyce uses the format — a mock‑scientific, mock‑theological Q&A — to expose Bloom’s private life with forensic neutrality. The tone is deliberately clinical, almost bureaucratic, which makes the content more revealing rather than more lurid.
The items you quoted belong to a subsection cataloguing:

• Bloom’s hidden erotic paraphernalia
• His curiosity about sexual practices
• His tendency to observe rather than act • His mingled shame, fascination, and tenderness

The key point: Joyce is not presenting Bloom as a deviant. He’s presenting him as human, with a private erotic imagination shaped by loneliness, voyeurism, and a desire to understand intimacy from multiple angles.
🔍 Why Joyce includes these specific images
Each item is chosen to illuminate a different facet of Bloom’s psychology:
1. “Low‑power magnifying glass”
A symbol of Bloom’s observational nature. He is a watcher, a detail‑noticer, someone who approaches sexuality through curiosity and analysis rather than dominance.
2. “Erotic photocards”
These are not presented as shocking but as part of Bloom’s private, melancholy erotic life. The two scenes Joyce selects are telling:

• a) A woman in the superior position
• b) A religious figure in a position of power over another
Both reflect Bloom’s recurring themes:

• female agency
• male passivity
• power dynamics
• the eroticization of humiliation
These echo what we see in Circe: Bloom’s fantasies often involve submission, being judged, or being placed in a subordinate role.
3. “Purchased by post from Box 32, Charing Cross”
This detail matters. It signals:

• Bloom’s isolation
• His discreet, almost timid approach to sexuality • The way he seeks connection through mediated, distant means
It’s the same psychological pattern behind his correspondence with Martha Clifford.
🧠 What this reveals about Bloom
This inventory is not about pornography. It’s about character.
It shows Bloom as:

• curious
• emotionally vulnerable
• drawn to scenarios where he is not in control • fascinated by the interplay of power, shame, and desire • gentle rather than aggressive

Joyce uses these objects to deepen Bloom’s humanity. They are artifacts of a man who feels excluded — from Molly, from Dublin, from traditional masculinity — and who processes that exclusion through a private erotic imagination that blends tenderness, humiliation, and observation.

blocks.label: The Bloom–Boylan connection
paras: Here’s the clean, high‑signal version of the Bloom–Boylan connection in Ulysses: what it is, how it works, and why Joyce makes it the emotional engine of the novel.
🔥 The Core: Boylan Is the Man Molly Is About to Sleep With
Bloom and Blazes Boylan are connected through Molly Bloom, Bloom’s wife. Boylan is:

• her concert manager
• her flirtation partner
• her imminent lover (their 4 p.m. rendezvous is the gravitational center of the whole book)

This affair is not hypothetical. It is happening today, June 16, 1904. Bloom knows it. Boylan knows Bloom knows it. And Molly knows Bloom knows it. That triangular awareness is the psychological architecture of the novel.
🎭 1. Boylan as Bloom’s Double and Opposite
Joyce builds Boylan as a foil—a kind of anti‑Bloom.

Bloom	Boylan
introspective, gentle, imaginative	physical, impulsive, swaggering emotionally intelligent	sexually confident empathetic	self‑satisfied
cerebral eroticism	bodily eroticism
Boylan is everything Bloom fears he is not. That’s why Boylan haunts Bloom’s thoughts all day.
💔 2. Boylan as the Embodiment of Bloom’s Cuckold Identity
Bloom’s relationship to Boylan is not just jealousy. It’s more complicated, more modern, more psychologically charged.
Bloom is:

• hurt by the affair
• aroused by the idea of Molly with another man • humiliated by Boylan’s swagger
• fascinated by Boylan’s masculinity
• compelled to imagine the encounter in vivid detail
This is why Boylan is not just a rival. He is the object of Bloom’s masochistic imagination.
Bloom’s erotic life is tied to submission, voyeurism, and humiliation. Boylan becomes the figure through which those desires crystallize.
🕒 3. The 4 p.m. Appointment as Narrative Clock
Boylan’s movements through Dublin are tracked like a comet:

• Bloom sees his name on posters
• hears people mention him
• imagines him buying fruit for Molly
• watches the clock approach 4 p.m.
Boylan becomes a temporal pressure. Every hour brings Bloom closer to the moment of betrayal.
This is why Boylan’s carriage ride to Eccles Street is one of the most suspenseful non‑events in modern literature.
🧠 4. Boylan Lives in Bloom’s Mind
Even when Boylan is not physically present, he is psychically present.
Bloom imagines:

• Boylan’s hands on Molly
• Boylan’s confident stride
• Boylan’s sexual prowess
• Boylan’s “jingle” (his signature rhythm)
Boylan becomes a kind of phantom rival, a projection of Bloom’s insecurities and fantasies.
🔥 5. In Circe, Boylan Becomes a Hallucinated Tormentor
In the hallucinatory “Circe” episode, Boylan appears as:

• a taunting, hypersexual figure
• a symbol of Bloom’s humiliation
• a theatrical exaggeration of Bloom’s fears
This is where the erotic and the humiliating fuse most explicitly. Boylan becomes the avatar of Bloom’s masochistic imagination.
🛏️ 6. After the Affair, Boylan’s Power Evaporates
Once the act is over, Boylan’s mythic presence collapses.
Molly’s monologue reveals:

• Boylan was not as impressive as Bloom imagined • she found him somewhat crude
• she still prefers Bloom emotionally and intellectually
Joyce flips the power dynamic. Boylan is a catalyst, not a replacement.
🎯 The Deep Connection
Boylan is not just Molly’s lover. He is:

• Bloom’s rival
• Bloom’s fantasy
• Bloom’s tormentor
• Bloom’s mirror
• Bloom’s erotic shadow
Their connection is psychological, erotic, symbolic, and structural. Boylan is the pressure that forces Bloom to confront who he is, what he desires, and what he fears.

blocks.label: Why the cuckold insecurity defines Bloom
paras:
In Ulysses, Bloom’s insecurity about being a "cuckold" (a man whose wife is unfaithful) isn't just a theory—it is the central psychological engine of the entire novel. June 16, 1904, is the day Bloom knows, with mathematical certainty, that his wife Molly will have an affair with her concert manager, Blazes Boylan. Here is why this insecurity defines his character: 1. The 4:00 PM Appointment
From the very first chapter featuring Bloom ("Calypso"), he sees a letter from Boylan to Molly. He knows they have an "appointment" at 4:00 PM at his own home. Throughout the day, he is constantly checking his watch, calculating where Boylan is, and trying to stay away from his own house to avoid the confrontation. 2. The "Someone in the House" Motif
As seen in the passage you quoted with the Bohee brothers, Bloom’s mind turns everything into a reminder of the affair. * The Song: "There’s someone in the house with Dina" is a direct mental projection of Boylan being in the house with Molly. * The Cuckoo: Later in the book, Joyce uses the sound of a "cuckoo" clock to mock Bloom, as the word "cuckold" is derived from the cuckoo bird (which lays its eggs in other birds' nests). 3. The "Envy" of the "Usurper"
Bloom views himself as physically inferior to Boylan. Boylan is loud, aggressive, "masculine" in a traditional sense, and successful. Bloom is quiet, scientific, and sensitive. * In the "Circe" episode, his insecurity reaches a fever pitch where he actually hallucinates watching the affair happen. * He imagines himself as a servant or a bystander, reflecting a deep sense of powerlessness and sexual humiliation. 4. Comparison to Othello
You noticed his mention of "Othello black brute." This is a key insight into his brain: * Othello is the most famous cuckold in literature (though he was falsely led to believe it). * By thinking of Othello, Bloom is processing his own jealousy. However, unlike Othello, who responds with murder and rage, Bloom responds with resignation and "equanimity." He tries to rationalize the affair as a "natural" event, though it pains him deeply. 5. The Lost Son
A major reason Bloom "allows" the affair to happen is his grief. Bloom and Molly haven't had a full sexual relationship since their infant son, Rudy, died eleven years earlier. Bloom feels he has "failed" as a father and a husband, which fuels his belief that he deserves to be replaced by a "stranger" like Boylan. Summary of Bloom's Cuckoldry
| Symptom | Evidence in the Text |
|---|---|
| Avoidance | He spends the entire day wandering Dublin to avoid his own front door. | | Physical Manifestation | He feels a "cold crust" or a physical weight in his chest when he thinks of Boylan. | | Hallucination | In "Circe," he sees Boylan’s face in mirrors or hears Boylan’s "jingling" carriage everywhere. |

blocks.label: Does Bloom enjoy it?
paras:
In the context of Leopold Bloom—and in the psychological study of the "cuckold" archetype in literature—the answer is complex. It isn't necessarily about "enjoyment" in a simple sense, but rather a tangled knot of masochism, resignation, and voyeurism. In Ulysses, Bloom’s reaction to Molly’s affair with Blazes Boylan functions on three distinct levels: 1. The Masochistic Hallucination
In the "Circe" episode you’ve been quoting, Bloom’s subconscious takes over. He doesn't just imagine the affair; he imagines himself helping Boylan. * He sees himself acting as a servant, holding a light for Boylan, or even peering through a keyhole. * This suggests a form of sexual masochism. By imagining the scene in such vivid, humiliating detail, Bloom is "mastering" his fear by leaning into the pain of it. 2. "Equanimity" (The Scientific Defense) When Bloom finally returns home in the "Ithaca" episode and sees the physical indentations in his bed made by Boylan, he conducts a mental "inventory" of his feelings. He lists them as: * Envy: That another man possesses what he does not. * Jealousy: The fear of replacement.
* Abnegation: The realization that he cannot change it. * Equanimity: The final state he reaches. He rationalizes the affair as a "natural" act—as inevitable as the tides or gravity. By turning the betrayal into a "scientific fact," he protects himself from the raw emotional devastation. 3. The "Shared" Experience
There is a theory in Joyce studies that Bloom finds a strange, vicarious connection to Molly through her lovers. Since Bloom has felt sexually "stunted" since the death of their son Rudy, he uses Boylan as a proxy. If Molly is happy and sexually satisfied, Bloom feels a lingering sense of connection to that vitality, even if he isn't the one providing it. 4. The Power Shift
While Bloom is often seen as "weak," his acceptance of the cuckold role can be interpreted as a form of survival. By not reacting with violence (like Othello) or leaving (like a traditional "alpha" male of 1904), he maintains his place in the house. He chooses the "humiliation" of being a cuckold over the "desolation" of being alone. Why "Circe" is so important here
The passage you quoted earlier—with the Bohee brothers singing—shows that Bloom’s mind is a "house" where he is never alone. He is always haunted by "someone in the house with Dina." For Bloom, the "enjoyment" is a defense mechanism; if he can find a way to be interested or titillated by his own betrayal, the betrayal loses its power to destroy him.
